name: Kapre
description: The Kapre is a giant, dark-skinned, tobacco-smoking tree-dwelling spirit of Philippine folklore, traditionally associated with large balete, acacia, and mango trees. Generally non-hostile but mischievous and territorial, the kapre is regarded as a guardian of its tree.
full_description: The Kapre is a class of tall, dark-skinned, hairy male giant of Philippine folklore, generally said to be 7–9 feet (2–3 m) tall, often shown wearing a bahag (loincloth), and almost always smoking a large cigar or pipe whose tobacco glow is one of the principal field-signs witnesses use to identify a kapre's presence. The kapre lives in large, old trees — most famously balete (Ficus species), acacia, mango, and bamboo — and is regarded as a guardian or 'owner' of that tree; cutting down a kapre's tree without first asking permission is said to bring misfortune. Kapres are usually mischievous rather than dangerous: they confuse travelers, cause people to lose their way in familiar surroundings, rustle branches when there is no wind, or (in some accounts) fall in love with a human and stalk them benignly. The word 'kapre' is a Spanish-period loan from cafre, ultimately from the Arabic kāfir ('infidel', 'non-believer'), a pejorative used by colonial Spaniards for dark-skinned peoples of the East Indies and Africa; the earliest attestation in the Philippine context is in Antonio Pigafetta's chronicle of the Magellan circumnavigation (chapri, recorded 1521). Modern folklorists generally read the kapre as a colonial-era racialization of indigenous forest-dwelling peoples (the Aeta / Agta, Mamanwa, and other Negrito groups) refracted into a forest-giant figure, layered onto deeper indigenous traditions of forest engkanto and tree-spirit guardians. The kapre remains a vivid figure in modern Filipino popular culture, present in komiks, films, the Trese graphic-novel and Netflix series (2021), and as a ubiquitous Halloween / town-fiesta character.

aliases.name: Kapre
aliases.language: Tagalog (loanword from Spanish cafre / Arabic kāfir)
aliases.meaning: From Spanish cafre, ultimately Arabic kāfir ('non-believer'); colonial-era pejorative reapplied to a folkloric giant

aliases.name: Agta
aliases.meaning: 'Black one' / dark-skinned forest giant; regional analogue of the kapre

aliases.name: Chapri
aliases.meaning: Earliest Spanish-language attestation, recorded by Antonio Pigafetta during the Magellan expedition

origin: Found throughout the Philippine archipelago, especially in lowland forests, rural barangays, and old agricultural land where balete and other large trees survive.

etymology.origin: Spanish cafre, from Arabic kāfir ('infidel'); applied during the colonial period in the Philippines and East Indies as a racial pejorative for dark-skinned peoples
etymology.meaning: Literally 'infidel / unbeliever'; in folkloric usage, redirected to denote a tall, dark-skinned tree-dwelling giant
etymology.first_use: Earliest Philippine-context attestation is 'chapri' in Antonio Pigafetta's account of the Magellan voyage (1521); 'kapre' as folkloric figure is documented from the Spanish colonial period onward

timeline.event: Antonio Pigafetta records the term 'chapri' in his account of the Magellan expedition's landing at Suluan / Homonhon, applied to dark-skinned, tattooed indigenous peoples
timeline.significance: Earliest Spanish-context attestation of the lexeme that becomes 'kapre'
timeline.source: Pigafetta, A. — Primo viaggio intorno al mondo (c. 1525)

timeline.event: End of Spanish colonial rule in the Philippines; the kapre figure has by this time become a fixture of lowland Christian Filipino folklore
timeline.significance: Transition point: folkloric figure inherited into modern Filipino tradition

timeline.event: Beginning of the Trese komiks anthology (Budjette Tan and Kajo Baldisimo), which features kapre and other Philippine yokai-class figures prominently
timeline.significance: Major modern pop-culture vehicle for the kapre

timeline.event: Netflix premieres the animated series 'Trese', adapted from the komiks; features kapre prominently
timeline.significance: Global popular-culture exposure for the kapre

related.name: Engkanto
related.description: Broad Philippine category of nature-spirit / enchanted being to which the kapre belongs

related.name: Agta (folkloric giant)

related.name: Cyclops / oni
related.description: Comparable forest-giant motifs in other cultures (the Greek cyclops, the Japanese oni)

cultural_notes: Belief in kapres remains common in rural Philippines as a living folk tradition of respecting trees and forest places; in urban contexts the kapre is largely treated as folkloric heritage.

sources.title: The Aswang Complex in Philippine Folklore
